laurier.resume: A very common hedge plant that has escaped into forests. Leaves and seeds release cyanide when crushed.
identification: Thick, shiny evergreen leaves, smell of bitter almond when crushed
Black fruits in upright clusters
usages: Eat nothing. Don't use its branches to cook food.

girolle.resume: A highly prized egg-yolk-yellow mushroom, often in groups under beech and oak.
identification: Uniform egg-yolk yellow, irregular funnel-shaped cap
Underside with thick, forked RIDGES running down the stem (no true gills)
Firm white flesh, apricot smell

sosies.diff: Brighter orange, true thin crowded gills, soft flesh. Indigestible.
Orange, in clumps on wood or stumps, true gills. Severe digestive upset.

usages: Have every harvest checked by a mycologist or a mycological society before eating.

piedmouton.resume: Recognisable by its underside covered in spines, with no known poisonous look-alike here.
identification: Cream to pale orange, irregular cap
Underside covered in small, fragile SPINES instead of gills
Brittle white flesh
usages: Get it checked before eating.

coulemelle.resume: A large umbrella mushroom of meadows and edges. Its small cousins, the Lepiotas, are deadly.
identification: Cap 15 to 30 cm covered with brown scales, a bump in the centre
Tall stem with brown snakeskin pattern and a double ring that slides
Free white gills

sosies.diff: Cap LESS than 10 cm, with pink to brown scales. Deadly: never a small Lepiota.
Smooth brown cap with white flakes, a rimmed volva at the base. Poisonous.

usages: Only eat caps over 15 cm, and after an expert has checked them.

trompette.resume: Despite its French name (“trumpet of death”), an excellent edible. Black, trumpet-shaped, under beech.
identification: Grey-black funnel, hollow down to the stem
Smooth or wrinkled outside, no gills
Grows in troops among dead leaves
usages: Get it checked before eating.

pleurote.resume: Grows in tiers on dead broadleaf wood, even in winter.
identification: Grey-blue to brown oyster-shaped caps, with little or no stem
White gills running down the stem
In overlapping clusters on trunks and stumps

sosies.diff: Sulphur-yellow caps in clumps on stumps, greenish gills, bitter taste. Poisonous.

usages: Get it checked before eating.

vesse.statut: Edible when young · get it checked
vesse.resume: A white ball that can reach the size of a football. The rule: always cut it in half.
identification: Large smooth white ball, no visible stem
Uniform white flesh, like mozzarella, when young

sosies.diff: Cut in half, it shows the outline of a mushroom (cap, gills, stem) inside. Deadly.

usages: Cut every specimen in half: the flesh must be white and uniform.
Get it checked before eating.

morille.resume: A spring mushroom with a cap pitted like a sponge. Poisonous raw.
identification: Honeycomb cap, joined to the stem
Completely hollow when cut in half

sosies.diff: Brain-like cap (folds), chambered inside, not hollow. Deadly.

usages: Always well cooked, never raw.
Get it checked before eating.

boletbai.resume: Very common under spruce and pine.
identification: Chestnut-brown cap, sticky in wet weather
Yellow pores that turn blue when touched
Light brown stem without a net pattern

sosies.diff: Pores that turn pink, dark net on the stem, very bitter taste.

usages: Get it checked before eating.

panthere.resume: Causes agitation, confusion and coma. Gets confused with edibles.
identification: Smooth brown cap dotted with white flakes
White gills, smooth ring
Bulb at the base with a clear rim
usages: Eat nothing.

vireuse.resume: The “angel of death”: entirely white, as deadly as the death cap.
identification: All white, cap often conical
Shaggy stem, fragile ring
White sac-like volva at the base

sosies.diff: White means nothing: a white mushroom is not necessarily edible.

usages: Eat nothing.

cortinaire.resume: Destroys the kidneys. Symptoms may only appear after several days.
identification: Tawny-orange mushroom, silky cap
Rust-coloured gills
Cobweb-like veil remains (cortina) on young ones
usages: Eat nothing.

entolome.resume: A large pale grey mushroom, often picked by mistake.
identification: Grey-cream cap, wavy edge
Yellowish gills turning salmon pink
Smell of flour
usages: Eat nothing.

hypholome.resume: The most common sulphur-yellow mushroom on stumps.
identification: Sulphur-yellow caps, more orange in the centre, in large clumps
Yellow-green gills turning blackish
Very bitter taste
usages: Eat nothing.

vipere.resume: The only viper of northern Europe. Discreet and rare, it only bites if handled or stepped on.
identification: Stocky snake 50 to 65 cm long
Continuous dark zigzag along the back
Vertical slit pupil

sosies.diff: Longer and slimmer, yellow and black collar behind the head, round pupil. Harmless.

usages: If bitten: stay calm, lie down, keep the limb still, remove rings and watch, disinfect.
Don't suck, cut or apply a tourniquet. Call 112.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, only in the south of Namur province (near Givet) and a reintroduction area in Liège province. Not known in the Ourthe valley.
notes.FR: Found mainly in the northern half, the Massif Central, the Jura and the Alps. Don't confuse it with the asp viper, further south.

loup.resume: Back in much of Western Europe. It avoids humans.
identification: Bigger than a German shepherd, grey-beige coat, dark back
Tracks: 4 toes, oval print 10 cm long, in a straight line
usages: Never feed or approach. Keep your dog on a lead.
Report a sighting to your region's nature services (see the country note).

notes.BE: Has returned naturally to Wallonia, with several areas of permanent presence. Report a sighting to the Réseau Loup (Service public de Wallonie).
notes.FR: Well established in the Alps, the Jura and the Massif Central, and spreading elsewhere.
notes.CH: Several packs in the Alps and the Jura.

chevreuil.resume: The most common deer. Barks when disturbed.
identification: Small deer, reddish in summer, grey-brown in winter
White patch on the rump (the “mirror”)
Tracks: small split hoof 4 to 5 cm
usages: A fawn on its own is not abandoned: never touch it.

blaireau.resume: Nocturnal, lives in clans in large setts.
identification: Black-and-white striped head
Tracks: 5 toes in a line with long claws
Latrines: small pits where it leaves its droppings
usages: Don't camp near an active sett.

salamandre.resume: Black and yellow, comes out on rainy nights in damp forests. A protected species threatened by a deadly fungus carried on hands and boots.
identification: Black amphibian with large yellow spots
Slow, moves at night in wet weather
usages: Don't handle it: its skin secretes an irritant, and you can pass a disease on to it.
Clean and dry your boots between two sites.

processionnaire.resume: Its microscopic hairs cause itching, eye irritation and sometimes breathing difficulties, even without direct contact.
identification: Hairy grey caterpillars in lines or clusters on oak trunks
Whitish silky nests on the bark
usages: Don't approach the nests, don't camp under an infested oak.
If contact: don't rub, rinse with water, change clothes.

frelon.resume: Stings are painful, and dangerous in case of allergy or multiple stings.
identification: Hornet: large (3 cm), reddish-brown and yellow
Wasp: yellow and black, narrow waist
usages: Don't leave sweet food open.
If the face swells, breathing gets difficult or you feel faint after a sting: call 112.

rosedespres.resume: The pasture mushroom, wild cousin of the button mushroom. Its confusions with white Amanitas are among the most serious.
identification: Silky white cap
PINK gills when young, then chocolate brown (never white)
Single ring, NO volva at the base
In grazed meadows, not in forests

sosies.diff: WHITE gills that stay white, sac-like volva at the base (dig out the stem). Deadly.
Turns bright yellow when you scratch the base of the stem, smell of ink or chemicals. Poisonous.

usages: Have every harvest checked by a mycologist or a mycological society before eating.

coprin.statut: Edible very young · get it checked
coprin.resume: Tall, scaly, shell-shaped white cap on banks and lawns. It dissolves into black ink within hours.
identification: Cylindrical white cap covered in woolly scales
White gills turning pink, then liquid black
Movable ring on the stem

sosies.diff: Smooth grey bell-shaped cap. Poisonous with alcohol up to 72 h after the meal.

usages: Only very young, gills still white, eaten the same day.
Get it checked before eating.

piedbleu.resume: A late-season violet mushroom in dead leaves and hedges.
identification: Lilac to violet-brown cap, smooth
Lilac, crowded gills
Violet stem, without ring or veil
Fruity smell

sosies.diff: Cobweb-like veil remains (cortina) under the cap, gills turning rust. Some webcaps destroy the kidneys.

usages: Always well cooked.
Get it checked before eating.

mousseron.resume: A white spring mushroom, often in rings in the grass, with a strong smell of flour.
identification: Thick, fleshy cream cap
Very crowded white gills
Strong smell of fresh flour
Grows in spring, in rings or lines

sosies.diff: Fibrous conical cap that turns red, fruity smell. Seriously poisonous (muscarine).
Yellowish gills turning salmon pink. Seriously poisonous.

usages: Have every harvest checked by a mycologist or a mycological society before eating.

fauxmousseron.resume: A small beige lawn mushroom, growing in “fairy rings”.
identification: Small beige cap with a bump
Widely spaced cream gills
Thin, tough stem: it twists without breaking
In rings on lawns

sosies.diff: Same lawns, powdery white cap, crowded gills running down the stem. Poisonous (muscarine).

usages: Have every harvest checked by a mycologist or a mycological society before eating.

armillaire.resume: Huge honey-yellow clumps on stumps and trees. Poorly tolerated by many people, even cooked.
identification: Tight clumps on wood or at the foot of trees
Honey-coloured caps dotted with small dark tufts
Cottony ring on the stem

sosies.diff: Smaller, in small clumps, without dark tufts. Deadly.
Sulphur yellow, greenish gills, no ring, very bitter. Poisonous.

usages: For experienced foragers only: never raw, always well cooked, in small amounts.
Get it checked before eating.

collybie.resume: One of the few mushrooms of deep winter, on dead wood, even after frost.
identification: Small orange caps, sticky and shiny
VELVETY stem, brown-black towards the base
In clumps on broadleaf wood, in winter

sosies.diff: Small ring on the stem, stem not velvety, matt cap. Deadly: a classic winter confusion.

usages: Have every harvest checked by a mycologist or a mycological society before eating.

oreillejudas.resume: A brown, gelatinous ear-shaped fungus, mostly on elder.
identification: Gelatinous, rubbery texture
Brown ear shape, velvety on top
On dead or living elder branches
usages: Always cooked.
Get it checked before eating.

polypore.resume: Large bright orange and yellow brackets on trunks. The “chicken of the woods”.
identification: Overlapping bright orange brackets edged with yellow
Sulphur-yellow underside full of pores
Tender flesh when young
usages: Only young and well cooked, in small amounts (intolerance is common).
Never if it grows on yew, black locust or a conifer.
Get it checked before eating.
